paragraphs.text: IV. AGAINST ADIMANTUS.

On the passage: "In the beginning God made heaven and earth," up to the words: "And there was evening and there was morning, one day." The utterly foolish Manichaeans hold that this chapter of the Law is opposed to the gospel. They say that Genesis records that God made heaven and earth and light by himself, whereas the gospel records that the world was fashioned through our Lord Jesus Christ, where it says: "And the world was made through him, and the world did not know him." They are refuted in three ways. First, when it says, "In the beginning God made heaven and earth," the Christian takes it of the Trinity itself, in which not the Father alone but also the Son and the Holy Spirit are understood. For we believe not in three gods but in one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, although the Father is the Father, the Son is the Son, and the Holy Spirit is the Holy Spirit. It would take too long to discuss the unity of the Trinity here. Second, where it says, "God said, Let it be, and it was made," we must understand that he made what he made through the Word. And the Word of the Father is the Son. So this chapter of Genesis, where it is written, "And God said, Let it be, and it was made," does not conflict with the passage of the gospel that says, "And the world was made through him," that is, through our Lord, since he is the Word of the Father, through whom all things were made. Finally, if the Son is not to be understood in Genesis because it does not say that God made things through the Son, then neither in the gospel does God feed the birds and clothe the lilies through the Son, nor do the countless other things that the Lord himself says God the Father does, since he does not say that the Father does them through the Son. They also bring in the testimony of the apostle, who says of our Lord Jesus Christ: "He is the firstborn of all creation; and all things were made through him in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible," and they say that this chapter is opposed to Genesis, where God is said to have made the world in such a way that the Son is not specifically named. They are badly mistaken, and they do not see that, if this were so, the apostle himself would contradict himself, since in another place he speaks of the one "from whom are all things, through whom are all things, in whom are all things," and does not name the Son. But just as the Son is not named there and yet is understood, so it is in Genesis; and just as these two chapters of Paul do not oppose each other, so neither does Genesis oppose the gospel.

On the passage: "And God finished on the sixth day all his works that he had made, and on the seventh he rested from all the same works of his that he had made." The Manichaeans also raise a false charge against this passage. They say that the statement in Genesis that God rested on the seventh day from all his works that he had made is opposed to the New Testament, because the Lord says in the gospel: "My Father is working until now." But there is no contradiction at all. The Lord was refuting the error of the Jews, who thought that God rested on the seventh day in such a way that from then on he did nothing whatever. He rested from all his works that he had made, in the sense that he would no longer make the world with everything in it, but not in the sense that he also rested from governing the world. For it is not written, "God rested from all works," so as to do no work thereafter; what is written is, "God rested from all his works that he had made," so that from then on he would work, not in making the world, a work he had ceased from once it was complete, but in governing it, and the Lord made known that he is engaged in this work. Nor does that rest mean that God sought a pause after toil. It means that he ceased from establishing the natures of things once those things were complete, although he is working even now in governing them.

The Jews, however, did not understand the observance of the sabbath; they thought that one had to cease even from works that serve people's well-being. For this reason the Lord refuted them in other places too, with a marvelous comparison about a sheep that has fallen into a well and a beast of burden that must be untied to be led to water. The sabbath was not repudiated by Christians but understood. They have indeed stopped observing it in a fleshly way, but the saints keep it spiritually, for they understand the voice of the Lord calling them to rest and saying: "Come to me, you who labor, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light." This is the sabbath, that is, this is the rest, that the scripture signified. The Jews did not understand it, and, in keeping with the ordering of the times, they followed in a fleshly way the shadow whose body, so to speak, that is, the truth, was to be given to us. And just as that rest of God is presented as coming after the world was fashioned, so we shall attain the rest promised to us after the works we do in this world, if they are just, namely in the seventh and last age of the world, which it would take too long to discuss. So the Lord does not cancel the scripture of the Old Testament but compels us to understand it; and he does not abolish the sabbath so that what it prefigured might perish, but rather opens it up so that what was hidden might come to light.

On the passage in Genesis: "And God said: It is not good for the man to be alone; let us make a helper for him. And God sent sleep upon Adam, and he fell asleep; and he took one of his ribs, from which he formed Eve, and brought her to Adam, and he said: Therefore a man will leave his father and mother and cling to his wife." Here again the Manichaeans raise a false charge. They say that this statement, in which God is described as forming the woman and joining her to the man, is contrary to the New Testament, because in the gospel the Lord says: "Everyone who leaves home or wife or parents or brothers or children for the sake of the kingdom of heaven will receive seven times as much in this time, and in the age to come will possess eternal life." I am amazed that they are so blind in this charge, or rather I am not amazed, for, as it is written, "their malice has blinded them." Yet who would fail to see how many commands the New Testament gives about loving one's wife? Why, then, do they say that it is the Old Testament that opposes this saying of the Lord, in which he says that a wife must be left for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, and not that the New Testament opposes itself? That would be wicked to say. Things that seem contradictory to the unlearned must be understood, not rashly accused.

For when the Jews asked the Lord whether he approved of sending a wife away with a certificate of divorce, he answered them: "Have you not read that he who made them at the beginning made them male and female, and said: For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two will be in one flesh? So they are no longer two but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined, let no man separate." And they said to him: "Why then did Moses command that a certificate of divorce be given and the wife sent away?" Jesus said to them: "Because of the hardness of your hearts Moses allowed you to send away your wives; but from the beginning it was not so. And I tell you: whoever sends away his wife, except on the ground of fornication, makes her commit adultery, and if he marries another, he himself commits adultery." Here they have the statement of the Old Testament confirmed by the Lord himself against the ignorance of the Jews. At the same time he bore witness to Moses, that he allowed divorce because of their hardness. Will they say that the gospel too contradicts the gospel? And if they say that this chapter is false and was added by corrupters of the scriptures (for that is what they usually say when they cannot find an answer), what then if someone else says that the passage they themselves cite, where the Lord says, "Everyone who leaves home or wife or parents or children for the sake of the kingdom of heaven," and so on, is an interpolation and false? The wretches do not understand how, in saying such things, they are trying to overturn the whole Christian faith. But the true faith and the teaching of the Catholic Church affirm that both are true and were spoken by the Lord, and are in no way contradictory, because both the union of husband and wife comes from the Lord, and leaving one's wife for the sake of the kingdom of heaven comes from the Lord. For although Jesus Christ raised the dead and gave them life, it does not follow that life itself is not to be given up for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. In the same way, although the Lord gave the wife to the husband, she must nevertheless be left, if need be, for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. For this is not always necessary, as the apostle says: "If any believer has an unbelieving wife and she consents to live with him, let him not send her away." This surely means that if she does not consent to live with him, that is, if she detests the faith of Christ in him and will not tolerate his being a Christian, she must be left for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, as the same apostle says further on: "But if the unbeliever departs, let him depart; for a brother or sister is not bound in such cases." So if a man forsakes the kingdom of heaven because he is unwilling to leave a wife who will not tolerate a Christian husband, the Lord condemns him; and likewise if a man leaves his wife with a certificate of divorce when there is no ground either of fornication or of gaining the kingdom of heaven, the Lord condemns him in the same way. Thus neither are these two gospel chapters found to contradict each other, nor does the gospel contradict the Old Testament, because there the wife is joined to the husband so that together they may be worthy to possess the kingdom of heaven; and so too the wife is commanded to be left if she hinders the husband from possessing the kingdom of heaven.

And that is why, when the apostle admonishes Christians of both kinds, that is, husbands and wives, does he not say: "Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her"? And: "Let wives be subject to their husbands as to the Lord, because the church too is subject to Christ"? And what these wretches mock in the Old Testament, the words, "Therefore a man will leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two will be in one flesh," does not the same apostle take as a great sacrament when he says: "This is a great sacrament, and I say it of Christ and the church"? Then he adds: "Nevertheless, let each one love his wife as himself, and let the wife fear her husband." Does he not show most plainly in another place that both the nature of each sex and their union are grounded in the Lord God, their creator and orderer, when he says: "Nevertheless, in the Lord neither is woman without man nor man without woman. For as woman came from man, so man comes through woman; but all things come from God"? If these people were willing to consider this, they would not throw darkness over the unlearned by setting certain chapters apart and fraudulently pitting them against one another; they would perceive that everything in both the Old and the New Testament was written and commended by the one Holy Spirit.

For in the Old Testament, too, they have in the prophet Isaiah how much is promised to eunuchs, lest they think these are praised by the Lord only in the New, where he says that there are some who have castrated themselves for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, and adds: "Let him who can accept it accept it." For Isaiah says this: "Thus says the Lord to the eunuchs who keep my commandments and choose for themselves what I will and hold fast to my covenant: I will give them in my house and within my wall a most renowned place, far better than sons and daughters; I will give them an everlasting name, and it will never fail." Before the Lord's coming, the people who received the Old Testament were held under certain shadows and figures of things, in accordance with a wonderful and perfectly ordered arrangement of the times; yet in it there is so much proclamation and foretelling of the New Testament that no commands or promises, however lofty and divine, are found in the gospel and the apostolic teaching that are lacking in those old books as well. But the holy scriptures call not for rash and proud accusers, but for careful and devout readers.

On the passage in Genesis: "And God said to Cain: What have you done? The voice of your brother's blood cries out to me from the earth. Now you are cursed from the face of the earth, which has swallowed and received your brother's blood from the slaughter by your hand; for you must till the earth, because it will give you barren fruits." The Manichaeans raise a false charge against this chapter of Genesis, in which Cain received a curse, to be punished by the barrenness of the earth, and in their eagerness to show it contrary to the gospel they truly seem to me to think they are dealing not with human beings at all, but as if those who listen to them or read their writings were cattle. So far have they abused their hearers' ignorance and slowness of wit, or rather their blindness of mind. For they said that what the Lord said to his disciples in the gospel is contrary to this chapter: "Do not take thought for tomorrow, for tomorrow will take thought for itself. Look at the birds of the air, for they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns." As if Cain, the murderer of his brother, were to be compared with the disciples of Christ, so that, because he deserved the punishment of a barren earth, it would follow that these too should suffer the same barrenness, men who followed our Lord Jesus Christ and were being prepared to preach the gospel! On the contrary, in these two chapters, one from Genesis and the other from the gospel, which they set out as hostile to each other, there is found such friendship and harmony that none greater could be wished for. What could be more fitting, what more appropriate, than that barrenness should pursue the man by whose crime his brother had been killed, even as he labored on the earth, while the earth should serve fruitfully those through whose ministry in preaching God's word their brothers were being set free, even though they took no thought at all for tomorrow? And if they shudder that in the Old Testament the earth was made barren for a sinner by God's curse, why do they not shudder in the New Testament that a fig tree was made to wither by the curse of our Lord Jesus Christ, though it had committed no sin against its Lord? Again, if they delight in the Lord's saying, in which he tells his disciples not to take thought for tomorrow, because God takes care of their food, why do they not also delight in the prophetic saying, which sang: "Cast your care upon the Lord, and he will feed you"? In this way, if they can, the wretches may understand both that the things they detest in the Old Testament as said of God are so right that they are found in the New as well, and that the things they praise and proclaim in the New are also found in the Old. From this the evident harmony of the two testaments will become clear to those who understand rightly.

On the passage in Genesis: "Let us make man in our image and likeness." The Manichaeans say that this passage in Genesis, where it is written that man was made in the image and likeness of God, is contrary to the New Testament, because in the gospel the Lord says to the Jews: "You are of your father the devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father; he was a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth, because the truth is not in him"; and because in another place the Jews are called a brood of serpents and vipers. They do not understand that the statement that man was made in the image and likeness of God was said of man before he sinned, whereas what is in the gospel, "You are of your father the devil," is said to sinners and unbelievers. For in the holy scriptures the term "sons" is used in three ways. One is according to nature, as Isaac was the son of Abraham, as are the rest of the Jews who come from the same origin. Another is according to teaching, so that someone is called the son of the person from whom he learned something in that matter, as the apostle calls those who learned the gospel from him his sons. The third is according to imitation, as the apostle calls us sons of Abraham because we imitate his faith. So the sinful and unbelieving Jews are called sons of the devil by the Lord in two ways: either because they learned impiety from him, as the apostle says of the devil himself, "who is now at work in the sons of unbelief"; or because they imitate him, which fits better with what was said of him, "and he did not stand in the truth," since the Jews too did not stand in the truth of the Law given to them, as the same Lord testifies when he says: "If you believed Moses, you would believe me too, for he wrote of me." And because of the venom of those same sins they are also called a brood of serpents and vipers.

But it is not only Genesis that proclaims that man was made in the image of God; the apostle does too, when he says: "A man ought not to veil his head, since he is the image and glory of God, but the woman is the glory of the man." And to make it plainly understood that man was made in the image of God not according to the oldness of sin, which is corrupted, but according to a spiritual conforming, the apostle likewise urges us to strip off the habit of sins, that is, the old man, and to put on the new life of Christ, which he calls the new man. And to teach that we once lost this, he calls it a renewal. For he speaks thus: "Stripping off the old man with his deeds, put on the new, who is being renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created him." So the sons of God are people renewed according to his image and made like him, even to the point of loving their enemies, as the Lord says that we ought to love our enemies so that we may be like our Father who is in heaven. And scripture teaches that God himself has placed this within our power when it says: "He gave them power to become sons of God." But people are called sons of the devil when they imitate his impious pride, fall away from the light and the height of wisdom, and do not believe the truth, people such as the Lord rebukes when he says: "You are of your father the devil," and so on. The prophet agrees with this passage of the gospel when he says: "I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High; but you will die like men, and fall like one of the princes."

On what is written in Exodus: "Honour your father and your mother." The Manichees also say that a passage of the Gospel contradicts this text, in which God commanded that parents be honoured. In that passage, when someone said, "Let me first go and bury my father," the Lord answered, "Let the dead bury their own dead; but you, come and proclaim the kingdom of God." This is resolved in the same way as the earlier passage, where it was said that a wife should be left for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. We ought to honour our parents, and yet we are guilty of no impiety when we set them aside for the sake of proclaiming the kingdom of God. If the Gospel contradicts the Old Testament because of this saying, then it also begins to contradict the Apostle, who urges children to honour their parents and parents to love their children. And not only that: the Lord himself would seem to contradict himself, which it is wicked to believe. For in another place he says to a man seeking eternal life, "If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments," and among them he mentions this one too: "Honour your father and mother." When these commandments have been fulfilled, one grows further into the love of God, in which all perfection lies, for the love of neighbour is a sure step towards the love of God. That is why, when the man answered, "All these commandments I have kept," the Lord told him that one thing was lacking if he wished to be perfect: to sell all that he had, give it to the poor, and follow him. From this it is clear that honour towards parents must be kept in its proper rank, and yet that, compared with the love of God, and above all if they stand in the way, parents must without any hesitation be set aside. In the old Scriptures, too, you find it written: "He who says to his father or mother, 'I do not know you,' and does not acknowledge his own children, has known your covenant." So if love of parents is commended in the New Testament, and setting parents aside is commended in the Old, then on both heads the two Testaments agree with each other.

On what is written in Exodus: "I am a jealous God, repaying the sins of the parents upon the children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me." The Manichees say that a passage of the Gospel contradicts this, where the Lord says, "Be kind, as your heavenly Father is, who makes his sun rise on the good and the evil," and also another saying of the Lord, that a brother who sins should be forgiven not only seven times but seventy times seven. Yet if I ask them whether God does not punish his enemies, they will no doubt be thrown into confusion. For they themselves say that God is preparing an eternal prison for the race of darkness, which they say is hostile to God. Nor is that all: they do not hesitate to say that he will also punish his own members together with that race. But when they come to passages of the Old and New Testaments, in order to deceive the unlearned and to accuse the Testaments of opposing each other, they pretend to be exceedingly good. Let them tell us, then: if he spares everyone and condemns no one, to whom will the Lord say, "Depart into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels"? We must therefore understand that this too was rightly said, that God will repay the sins of the parents upon the children who hate him. From the words he added, "of those who hate me," we understand that those are punished for their parents' sins who have chosen to persist in the same perversity as their parents. Such people are punished not by God's cruelty but rather by his justice and by their own wickedness, as the prophet says: "For the holy spirit of discipline will flee from deceit, and will withdraw from thoughts that are without understanding, and will be rebuked when iniquity comes upon it"—that is, a person will be rebuked when his own iniquity comes upon him, once the Holy Spirit has departed from him. And in another place: "These things they thought, and they went astray; for their own malice blinded them." And in another place: "Each one is bound fast by the cords of his own sins." With these testimonies of the Old Testament the Apostle agrees in the New, saying, "God handed them over to the desires of their hearts." This agreement of the two Testaments shows clearly enough that God is not cruel, but that each person is cruel to himself by sinning.

As for the statement that the punishment extends to the third and fourth generation, I think it signifies nothing other than this: from Abraham himself, who begins to be the father of the Jewish people, there are four ages, including the present one, and the evangelist Matthew distinguishes them. The first runs from Abraham to David, the second from David to the deportation to Babylon, the third from the deportation to Babylon to the coming of the Lord; from then until the end is reckoned the fourth, the old age of the world, as it were, longer than the other ages. We believe that these ages are meant by "generations," although each of them is made up of many generations. Now the third begins with the deportation to Babylon, when the Jews were taken captive, and in the fourth, that is, after the coming of our Lord, the Jewish nation was utterly uprooted from its own soil. So we are given to understand that the saying that God will repay the sins of the parents to the third and fourth generation applies, lawfully and deservedly, to those who chose to cling stubbornly to their parents' sins rather than follow the justice of God. For the prophet Ezekiel shows most plainly that a father's sins do not pass to a son who lives justly.

What is said in the Gospel, "Be kind, as your heavenly Father is, who makes his sun rise on the good and the evil," is not contrary to the Old Testament. God does this in order to invite people to repentance, as the Apostle says: "Do you not know that God's patience invites you to repentance?" Yet we must not therefore believe that God will not punish those who, as the same Apostle says, "store up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the just judgement of God, who will repay each one according to his works." The prophet too proclaims this patience and goodness of God, saying, "But you spare all things, because they are yours, you who love souls," and there are countless other passages. From them we understand that both Testaments proclaim God's mercy and justice, in his goodness and in his severity alike.

If they are troubled by the words "I am jealous," let them also be troubled by what the apostle Paul said: "I am jealous over you with the jealousy of God; for I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ." Holy Scripture, speaking in our words, shows through these very words that nothing can be said worthily of God. Why indeed should such words not be used of that majesty, when whatever is said of it is said unworthily, since it surpasses all the resources of every language by its inexpressible sublimity? Because husbands commonly guard their wives' chastity by being jealous, the Scriptures have called the power and discipline of God, by which he does not allow the soul to commit fornication with impunity, the jealousy of God. The soul's fornication is its turning away from the fruitfulness of wisdom and its turning towards conceiving temporal enticements and corruptions.

When the Lord says that a brother should be forgiven not only seven times but seventy times seven, he is of course speaking of one who repents. But God said that he repays sins to those who hate him, not to those who are reconciled to him through repentance. For the Lord also says through the prophet, "I do not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he turn and live." From this it is easy to see that in the patience that invites to repentance, in the mercy that pardons the penitent, and in the justice that punishes those who refuse to be corrected, both Testaments agree and harmonise with each other, as having both been written by one God.

On what is written in Exodus: "An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth," and other such things. The Manichees cavil at this passage, because the old Law permits equal retaliation and says that an eye must be lost for an eye and a tooth for a tooth, as if the Lord himself had shown these two to be opposed and contrary to each other in the Gospel. For he says: "You have heard that it was said to those of old, 'An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.' But I say to you, do not resist evil; but if anyone strikes you on the cheek, offer him the other as well; and if anyone wants to go to law with you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well." These two sayings do indeed show the difference between the two Testaments, but both were nevertheless established by one God. Because carnal people at first burned to avenge themselves far beyond the injury they complained of, the first step of gentleness was laid down for them: that the resentment of the avenger should in no way exceed the measure of the injury received. In this way a person who had first learned not to exceed an injury might in time be able to forgive it. So the Lord, now leading his people through the grace of the Gospel to the fullness of peace, built a second step upon this one, so that a person who had already heard that he should not repay more than he had suffered might, with a calm mind, gladly forgive the whole. The prophet proclaims this too in those old books, saying, "O Lord my God, if I have done this, if there is iniquity in my hands, if I have repaid those who repaid me with evil." And another prophet says of such a man, who suffers injuries and bears them with the utmost gentleness: "He will give his cheek to the one who strikes him; he will be filled with reproaches." From this we understand both that a measure of retaliation was rightly laid down for carnal people, and that complete forgiveness of injury was not only commanded in the New Testament but foretold long before in the Old.

On what is written, that God spoke with Adam and Eve, with the serpent, with Cain and with others of old. Of some of these it is also written that he appeared to them and was seen by them, and this not in one but in many passages of Scripture, where God is found both to have spoken with human beings and to have appeared to some of them. The Manichees therefore lie in wait and say that all of this is contrary to the New Testament, since the Lord says, "No one has ever seen God except the only Son, who is in the bosom of the Father; he has made him known to us," and again, when he says to the Jews, "You have never heard his voice nor seen his face, and you do not have his word abiding in you, because you have not believed the one whom he sent." We reply that the whole question can be resolved by the very words written in the Gospel: "No one has ever seen God except the only Son, who is in the bosom of the Father; he has made him known to us." For the Son himself, who is the Word of God, made the Father known to whom he willed—not only in these last times, when he deigned to appear in the flesh, but also before, from the founding of the world—whether by speaking or by appearing, either through some angelic power or through any creature whatever. For he himself is the truth in all things; all things hold together in him, and all things serve him at his nod and are subject to him, so that he appears even to bodily eyes, through a visible creature, to whom he wills when he deigns to do so. Yet in his divinity, and as the Word of the Father, coeternal with the Father and unchangeable, through whom all things were made, he is seen only by a heart that is utterly pure and single. That is why in certain places Scripture itself testifies that an angel was seen where it says that God was seen. So in Jacob's wrestling, the one who appeared is also called an angel. And when God appeared to Moses in the bush, and again in the desert when he had already led the people out of the land of Egypt and Moses received the Law, God spoke to him. Yet whether in the bush, when he sent him, or afterwards, when he gave him the Law, Stephen in the Acts of the Apostles says that an angel appeared to him. We say this so that no one may suppose that the Word of God, through whom all things were made, can be confined to places, as it were, or appear visibly to anyone except through some visible creature. For just as the Word of God is in a prophet, and it is rightly said, "The prophet said," and likewise rightly said, "The Lord said," because the Word of God, which is Christ, speaks the truth in the prophet, so too he himself speaks in an angel when the angel announces the truth. And it is rightly said, "God said" and "God appeared," and equally rightly said, "The angel said" and "The angel appeared," since the one is said in the person of God who dwells within, the other in the person of the creature that serves. By this rule the Apostle also says, "Or do you want proof of Christ, who speaks in me?"

If they are troubled that in the Old Testament God speaks even to sinners—to Adam, to Eve, to the serpent—let them also consider the kind of example the Lord gave in the New Testament about the foolish and greedy man, and how the Lord spoke to him, saying, "Fool, this night your soul will be taken from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?" For when the truth is spoken even to sinners, through whatever creature it is spoken, it is spoken by none other than him who alone is true. When he says to the Jews, "You have never heard his voice," he says it because those particular people with whom he was speaking did not obey. To them he also says, "Nor have you seen his face," because it cannot [?]. And he says, "Nor do you have his word abiding in you," because in whomever the Word of God abides, Christ abides in him, and these people rejected Christ. For when the Lord himself had said, "Father, glorify me with the glory that I had with you before the world was made," a voice sounded from heaven: "I have glorified it, and I will glorify it." Many of the Jews who were present heard that voice, and yet they are not to be said to have heard it, because they did not obey so as to believe. Therefore, if it is not to be wondered at that the Word of God, that is, the only Son of God, who makes the Father known, does so to whom he wills by himself and to whom he wills through some creature, whether by sound or by appearance, while he himself is seen in himself by a pure heart, and through him the Father—for "blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God"—then it is not to be wondered at that all these testimonies from both Testaments are in harmony.

On the passage where it is written that God spoke to Moses and said to him: “Speak to the children of Israel: Take first-fruits from every man, which you shall set apart for me, that is, gold, silver, bronze, purple, fine linen, scarlet, goats’ hair, rams’ skins dyed red, sound wood, oil for the lamps, incense, and precious stones, that is, beryls; and set up a tabernacle in which I may dwell with you.” From this too the Manichees raise a question, and they say that this passage of the Scriptures is contradicted by what the Lord says in the Gospel: “You shall not swear, either by heaven, for it is the throne of God, or by the earth, for it is his footstool.” For they argue, and think they are saying something great, when they say: “How does that God, whose throne is heaven and whose footstool is the earth, dwell in a tabernacle made of gold or silver and bronze and purple and the hair and skins of animals?” They even bring in the apostle Paul as a witness, because he says that God dwells in unapproachable light. We put to them a matching question, and what they have brought forward from the New Testament we bring forward from the Old. For there it was written first: “Heaven is my throne, the earth is my footstool: what house will you build for me, or what is the place of my rest? Did not my hand make all these things?” See, here they have a place where the books of the Old Testament proclaim that God does not dwell in temples made by hands. And yet the Son of our God, with a whip made of cords, drove out of the temple those who were selling oxen and doves, overturned the tables of the money-changers, and said: “My Father’s house shall be called a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of robbers.” Suppose, then, that someone set these two passages against each other as well, wishing to deceive the unlearned, and said that in the Old Testament God is magnified, whose throne is said to be heaven and whose footstool the earth, and who is denied to dwell in a house made by hands, while in the New Testament a temple built by men is called his house. Will not the Manichees admit, however belatedly, that in both Testaments a dwelling of God made by human hands is to be taken as signifying something, and that in both Testaments it is proclaimed that God does not dwell in places built by men?

On the passage written in Exodus: “Do not worship foreign gods,” and again: “Your God is called jealous; for he is jealous with jealousy.” When the Manichees find fault with this passage, where it is written, “Do not worship foreign gods,” they show plainly enough that they are pleased to have many gods worshipped. Nor is that surprising, since in their sect they speak of and commend a most numerous family of gods. Indeed they have even come down to these visible things, which they venerate and worship in place of the light of truth itself; and so they are displeased by what is written in Exodus: “Do not worship foreign gods.” They add that this too was said for the same reason: “Your God is called jealous; for he is jealous with jealousy,” so that we should not love God as a jealous God, since his jealousy does not allow us to be zealous for foreign gods. And so they say that these words are contrary to the Gospel, because the Lord says: “Righteous Father, the world has not known you,” as though God could not be called righteous unless he allowed us to worship foreign gods. For they argue that a righteous God and a jealous God are, as it were, contrary to each other, and they deceive wretched people who do not understand that the whole hope of our salvation is the jealousy of God. For by this name is signified that providence of his by which he allows no soul to commit fornication away from him with impunity, as the prophet says: “You will destroy all who commit fornication away from you.” For just as what is called the wrath of God is not a disturbance of mind but the power to punish, so the jealousy of God is not that torment of spirit by which a husband is usually racked against his wife or a wife against her husband, but a most tranquil and pure justice, by which no soul is allowed to be happy that is corrupted and, in a manner of speaking, made pregnant by false opinions and perverse desires. Those people shudder at these words who have not yet seen that no words are fitting for the ineffable majesty of God. They think one should refrain from these words as though, by not saying them, they were saying something worthy of God. But the Holy Spirit, intimating to people of understanding this very point, how ineffable are the highest divine things, chose to use even those words which among men are usually counted as faults, so that they might be reminded by this that even the things which people think they say with some dignity befitting God are unworthy of his majesty, to which an honouring silence would be more suitable than any human voice. I look for jealousy in a man, and I find a disturbance that torments the heart. Yet when I look for its cause, I find nothing other than that he cannot bear his spouse’s adultery; for jealousy is chiefly and properly spoken of between spouses. So if a husband were happy in himself, almighty and just, he would punish his spouse’s sin without any torment, with complete ease and with no injustice. And yet in the human manner of speaking I would call that action of his jealousy, if not properly, then figuratively and rightly. For who has found fault with Tully, who certainly knew how to speak Latin, when he said to Caesar: “Of all your virtues none is more admirable or more welcome than your mercy”? And yet they say that mercy (misericordia) is so called because it makes the heart (cor) of one who grieves at another’s misery wretched (miserum). Does a virtue, then, make the heart wretched? What, then, would Tully answer to such fault-finders, except that by the name of mercy he meant to speak of clemency? For we rightly speak not only by using proper words but also by borrowing neighbouring ones. I wanted to mention this author because the question is not about the thing but about the word. For just as our authors, namely those of the divine writings, were chiefly concerned with things, so almost all the care of worldly authors is for words. But I have the Gospel and all the books of the New Testament, in which the mercy of God is very frequently commended. If, then, these wretched people dare, let them raise a question from there too, and deny that God is merciful, lest he be understood to have a wretched heart. So just as there can be mercy in God without wretchedness of heart, so let us not disdain to accept the jealousy of God without any wasting or torment of spirit, and let us bear with the limitations of human speech, so that we may come to the divine silence. But if they say that a jealous God and a righteous God are contraries, what will they say when I find in the New Testament too: “I am jealous for you with the jealousy of God,” and also the testimony drawn from the Old and used in the Gospel: “Zeal for your house has consumed me”? And again, when they read in the Old: “The Lord is righteous and has loved righteousness; his face has beheld equity,” will they not admit that in this way too the two Testaments can seem contrary to the unlearned, since in the New we find the jealousy of God and in the Old the righteousness of God, whereas to those who understand rightly both are found in both, harmonizing in the great unity and peace of the Holy Spirit?

On the passage where it is written that blood must not be eaten, because the blood is the soul of the flesh. Against this precept of the old law the Manichees set what the Lord says in the Gospel, that we are not to fear those who can kill the body but cannot harm the soul; and they argue, saying: “If blood is the soul, how is it that men have no power over it, when they do many things with blood, whether catching it and setting it out as food for dogs and birds, or pouring it out, or mixing it with mud and mire?” For men can do these and countless other things with blood without difficulty. So they ask mockingly how, if the soul belongs to the blood, a man’s killer cannot harm the soul, when he has such great power over its blood. They add also what the apostle Paul says, that “flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God,” and they say: “If blood is the soul, as Moses says, no soul will be found able to attain the kingdom of God.” The first answer to this slander must be to compel them to show where it is written in the books of the old law that the human soul is blood. For they will nowhere find this in that Scripture which, for as long as the wretches try to tear it to pieces, they are in no way permitted to understand. But if nothing of the kind is said there about the human soul, what does it matter to us whether the soul of a beast can be harmed by a killer or cannot possess the kingdom of God? But because these people are overly anxious about the souls of beasts — for though human souls are rational, they nonetheless think they are returned into beasts — they suppose that the kingdom of heaven is closed to themselves if they agree that it is closed to the souls of beasts.

What of the fact that Adimantus, one of Mani’s disciples, whom they record as having been a great teacher of that sect, even dared to mock the people of Israel? He dared, then, to mock the Jewish people on the ground that, according to their understanding, by which they suppose blood to be the soul, the souls of their own forefathers were partly devoured by serpents, partly consumed by fire, and partly dried up in deserts and in the roughest places of the mountains. Even if anyone granted that this were true, he would prove that it happened without any crime on the part of those he wished to mock. For they did not themselves in any way harm the souls of their forefathers, to whom he said all those things had happened according to their understanding; so they can have grief over it, but not guilt. But what will Adimantus himself do, according to his own opinion, by which he believed that even rational souls, that is, the souls of men, can be thrust into the bodies of beasts? What will he do about so great a crime, whenever he wore out with blows a sluggish beast of burden, or one urged on with the bridle, in which perhaps his father’s soul may have been? Not to mention that he may even have killed his own parents among the lice and fleas, from the killing of which these people do not refrain. For what good does it do them that they sometimes deny that human souls can be returned into these tiniest of creatures? They deny it so as not to be held guilty of so many killings, or be forced to spare fleas and lice and bedbugs and to endure such great annoyance from them without any licence to kill them. For they are hard pressed to say why a human soul can be returned into a little fox but not into a weasel, when a fox cub is perhaps even smaller than a large weasel. Next, if it can go into a weasel, why not into a mouse? And if into that, why not into a lizard? And if into that, why not into a locust? Then into a bee, then into a fly, then into a bedbug, and from there all the way down to a flea, and to anything else much tinier still? For they cannot find where to set the limit, and so, through this frivolous cruelty, their consciences are buried under the crimes of countless homicides.

Now, as to what is written, that the blood of a beast is its soul: besides what I said above, that what becomes of a beast’s soul is no concern of mine, I can also interpret that precept as having been given as a sign. For the Lord did not hesitate to say, “This is my body,” when he was giving a sign of his body.

As for the apostle’s saying, “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God,” it was also said in the law: “My spirit shall not remain in these, because they are flesh.” And so often in the old books a future reward is promised to the souls of the righteous. But the apostle wished to convey what sort of body the righteous will have through transformation in the resurrection, since they will neither marry nor take wives but will be like the angels in heaven. Wishing, then, to convey this future transformation of the bodies of the saints, the apostle said: “For I tell you, brothers, that flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God.” This can be discovered not from a single sentence detached and cited for deceit, but by going through, or rather simply reading, that whole passage of the letter — for the matter is not obscure. For he says: “This corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.” That he says this of the body is plainly found from what precedes, when he says: “Not all flesh is the same flesh: there is one flesh of men, another of beasts, another flesh of birds, another of fish; and there are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies; but the glory of the heavenly is one and that of the earthly another; there is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory. So also is the resurrection of the dead. The body is sown in corruption, it will rise in incorruption; it is sown in dishonour, it will rise in glory; it is sown in weakness, it will rise in power; it is sown an animal body, it will rise a spiritual body. If there is an animal body, there is also a spiritual one, as it is written: The first man Adam became a living soul, the last Adam a life-giving spirit. But it is not the spiritual that is first, but the animal, and afterwards the spiritual. The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man is from heaven, heavenly. As was the earthly, so are those who are earthly; and as is the heavenly, so are those who are heavenly. And as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of him who is from heaven. Now this I say, brothers, that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor will corruption inherit incorruption.” Surely it is now clear why the apostle said this. Why, then, does this man, by so shameful a deceit, cite nothing but this last sentence and keep silent about what precedes, by which what he misinterprets could be rightly understood? For since the body of our Lord after the resurrection was so raised into heaven that it received a heavenly transformation suited to its heavenly dwelling, and we have been bidden to hope for this on the last day, the apostle said: “As was the earthly, so are those who are earthly,” that is, mortal; “and as is the heavenly, so are those who are heavenly,” that is, immortal not only in soul but also in body. That is why he had said above that the glory of heavenly bodies is one and that of earthly bodies another. And when he says that the body in the resurrection will be spiritual, we must not therefore think that it will not be a body but a spirit; rather, he calls it a spiritual body because it will be wholly subject to the spirit, without any corruption or death. For just because the body we now have is called animal, we must not think that it is not a body but a soul. So just as the body is now called animal because it is subject to the soul, but cannot yet be called spiritual because it is not yet fully subject to the spirit so long as it can still be corrupted, so then it will be called spiritual, when it will be unable to resist the spirit and eternity through any corruption.

Or if it still seems insufficiently shown that the apostle spoke that sentence on account of the transformation that is to come, when he said, “Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor will corruption inherit incorruption,” notice what he immediately adds and joins to it: “Behold, I tell you a mystery: we shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed, in an instant, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed.” Then he continues and says also what I mentioned a little earlier, to show what that transformation will be like. For he says at once: “For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.” From this, then, it is clear why flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God: because when it has put on incorruption and immortality, it will no longer be flesh and blood, but will be changed into a heavenly body. We have dealt with this incidentally, because those who deny the resurrection of bodies are also much in the habit of laying traps with this sentence. For this question was raised not about the body but about the soul, which they think is taken in the law in such a way that it is supposed to be blood — which we in no way understand so. But although we are not concerned about the souls of beasts, with which we have no fellowship of reason, nevertheless we say that what the law says, that blood is to be poured out and not taken as food because the blood is the soul, was given as a sign, just as many other things — indeed almost all the sacraments of those Scriptures — are full of signs and figures of the preaching that was to come, which has now been made plain through our Lord Jesus Christ. For the blood is the soul in the same way that the rock was Christ, as the apostle says: “For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ.” It is well known that the children of Israel drank water in the desert when the rock was struck, and it was of them that the apostle was speaking when he said this. Yet he did not say, “The rock signified Christ,” but, “The rock was Christ.” And lest this in turn be taken carnally, he calls it spiritual, that is, he teaches that it is to be understood spiritually. It would be a long task, and not necessary now, to explain the sacraments of that same law, except where it can be done briefly. It is enough that those who slander them should know that we do not understand them in the way they are accustomed to ridicule, but in the way the apostles, who understood everything, explained a few things, so as to leave the rest to be understood by later generations according to the same rules.

On the passage written in Deuteronomy: “See that you do not forget the covenant of your God which he wrote down, and make for yourselves likenesses and images”; and it adds further: “Your God is a devouring fire and a jealous God.” This is the way that Adimantus set out these words from the Scriptures; for it is his slanders that we have undertaken to refute and rebut. But I think enough has already been said in reply above, when he was slandering the jealousy of God. Let us remember, however, that not only there but here too he accused the Scriptures over the jealousy of God in such a way as to add also what is commanded in those books by the Lord our God about not worshipping idols, as though he found fault with God’s jealousy for no other reason than that by that very jealousy we are forbidden the worship of idols. So he wants to appear to favour idols. They do this in order to win for their most wretched and insane sect the goodwill of the pagans too. Against this chapter of the law they also set the passage where someone came to the Lord and said to him: “Good Master, what must I do to possess eternal life?” Jesus answered him: “Why do you ask me about what is good? No one is good but God alone.” From this, of course, we are meant to conclude that these are contradictory, because in the law it says, “God is a devouring fire,” and, “God is jealous,” but in the Gospel, “No one is good but God alone.”

About jealousy, we have already answered that these words are not set down in the Scriptures to signify any disturbance or torment in God. Rather, because nothing worthy can be said of God, Scripture has come down even to words like these. People think such words are unworthy, and so they are forced to learn that even the things they believe they say fittingly of the ineffable divine excellence are unworthy of God's majesty. Since God's Wisdom was going to descend to a human body, it first descended to human words. But when I begin to examine that word, I see that I have not spoken properly. Nothing can descend unless it can also move from place to place, for whoever descends seems to leave a higher place and make for a lower one. God's Wisdom, however, is wholly present everywhere, and so it can in no way pass from place to place. John speaks of it better in the Gospel, as one who shared the Lord's breast. He says: "He was in this world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him." And yet he also adds: "He came to his own, and his own did not receive him." How was he here, and how did he come? Only because that ineffable sublimity has to be signified by human sounds so that it may suit human beings. But insofar as it makes human beings gods, it must be understood in divine silence. So a reason can be given why it was said in this way. Yet nothing can be said worthily of God, for whatever could be said is unworthy by that very fact. Take error and pain away from jealousy, and what will remain except a will that guards chastity and punishes the corruption of marriage? What word, then, could better convey this than God's jealousy? We are called to marriage with God, and he does not want us to be corrupted by shameful love. He punishes our unchastity and loves chastity. It is not for nothing that people commonly say: "Whoever is not jealous does not love."

The words "a devouring fire" also belong here. I should not argue about them. Instead I should ask these people themselves what fire the Lord said he had come to send into this world. This is said in the Gospel, which they cannot attack, not because they want to honor Christ but because they want to deceive Christians. When we remind them that the Lord said, "I came to send fire into this world," the wretches reply: "But that is something different." We answer them: "And this is something different too. Do not be afraid." For Christ himself speaks in the Old Testament as well when he says, "I am a devouring fire." He is the same one who says in the Gospel that he came to send fire into this world, and that fire is the Word of God, which he himself is. After the resurrection he explained the old Scriptures to his disciples, beginning from Moses and all the prophets. Then the disciples themselves admitted that they had received fire, for they said: "Was not our heart burning on the way, when he opened the Scriptures to us?" He himself is the devouring fire, for divine love consumes the old life and renews a person. Because God is a devouring fire, he makes us love him, and because he is jealous, he himself loves us. So do not fear the fire that is God. Fear the fire that God has prepared for heretics.

Adimantus also picked a passage from the Gospel to throw before the unlearned as if it contradicted this chapter of the Law, the place where the Lord says, "No one is good but God alone." But how often is God's goodness found in the Old Testament! Who could count the passages? I will give just one, which is sung every day in the churches: "Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever." Surely this too seems contrary to a jealous God, as the Manichees think of him, and yet it is sung from the books of the Old Testament. Consider also that king who was holding a wedding for his son. Among the guests at table he found a man without a wedding garment. He first addressed him as "friend," then ordered him bound hand and foot and thrown into the outer darkness. To people who understand perversely, that king does not seem good. Suppose someone put forward that very chapter of the Gospel and slandered the Gospel the way Adimantus slanders the Old Testament. He would praise instead the books of the Old Testament, where it is written, "Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever," and he would find fault with the New because an invited guest is sent to such punishment over a garment. Suppose he did this tirelessly and with deceitful perversity, collecting all the gentle passages from the Old Testament and all the severe ones from the New, insisting that they were opposed to each other, praising the Old and condemning the New. He too would find unlearned people, pitifully ignorant of the divine Scriptures, whom he could persuade to keep the Old Testament rather than the New. These men do the same thing from the other side, attacking the Old Testament as though it were contrary to the New. I am amazed that they do not consider that someone may one day read both, understand both with God's help, and praise both. Such a reader will grieve over their deceit and malice as the deceit of fellow human beings, guard against it as the deceit of heretics, or laugh at it as the deceit of ignorant and proud men.

On what is written in Deuteronomy: "According to the desire of your soul, kill and eat all meat, according to the pleasure that the Lord has given you. But take care not to eat the blood; pour it out like water on the ground." Adimantus thinks these words of the Law are contradicted by what the Lord says in the Gospel: "Let not your hearts be weighed down with overindulgence and drunkenness and the cares of this world." He also thinks they are contradicted by what the apostle says: "It is good not to eat meat or drink wine," and again: "You cannot share in the table of the Lord and the table of demons." We, however, say that all these passages, whether written in the Old Testament or in the New, were set down because their own circumstances required them, and we show that they are not opposed to one another. Yet Adimantus himself could have noticed, in the very words he quoted from the Old Testament, that the command "According to the desire of your soul, kill and eat all meat" has nothing to do with unrestrained gluttony, since it continues: "according to the pleasure that the Lord has given you." The Lord has not given you unrestrained pleasure, only as much as is enough to sustain nature and keep you healthy. Whoever gives himself to unrestrained gluttony follows his own vice, not the pleasure the Lord has given. So the words set down in the Gospel are not contrary: "Let not your hearts be weighed down with overindulgence and drunkenness and the cares of this world." When someone satisfies only the pleasure the Lord has given, a pleasure that is moderate and natural, his heart is not weighed down with overindulgence and drunkenness and the cares of this world.

Now consider what the apostle says about not eating meat and not drinking wine. He did not give this command because he thought those things unclean, as these men suppose. They are in error themselves, and they hurl into error the people they have persuaded of such things. But since the apostle himself gave the reason why he said this, we need not interpret or explain the saying. It is enough to join the whole passage from the apostle's letter to this discussion. Then two things will plainly appear: the reason why the apostle said this, and the deceit of these men, who pick out scraps of Scripture to deceive the unlearned and do not connect them with what is written before and after, from which the writer's will and intention could be understood. This, then, is what the apostle says: "Welcome the one who is weak in faith, but not for disputes over opinions. One person believes he may eat anything, but let the one who is weak eat vegetables. Let the one who eats not despise the one who does not eat, and let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats, for God has welcomed him. Who are you to judge someone else's servant? It is before his own master that he stands or falls. And he will stand, for the Lord is able to make him stand. One person judges between days, another judges every day alike. Let each be fully convinced in his own mind. Whoever observes the day observes it for the Lord. Whoever eats, eats for the Lord, for he gives thanks to God. And whoever does not eat abstains for the Lord and gives thanks to God. For none of us lives for himself, and none of us dies for himself. If we live, we live for the Lord; if we die, we die for the Lord. So whether we live or die, we belong to the Lord. For this is why Christ died and rose again, so that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living. Why, then, do you judge your brother? Or why do you despise your brother? For we shall all stand before the judgment seat of the Lord. For it is written: 'As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God.' So each of us will give an account of himself. Let us therefore no longer judge one another. Judge this instead: never to put a stumbling block or an occasion of offense in a brother's way. I know and am convinced in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean through him. But to anyone who thinks something is unclean, it is unclean to him. If your brother is grieved because of food, you are no longer walking in love. Do not by your food destroy someone for whom Christ died. So do not let what is good for us be spoken of as evil. For the kingdom of God is not food and drink but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit. Whoever serves Christ in this way pleases God and is approved by people. Let us therefore pursue what makes for peace and for building one another up. Do not destroy the work of God for the sake of food. All things are indeed clean, but it is wrong for a person to eat in a way that causes offense. It is good not to eat meat or drink wine or do anything that makes your brother stumble. Keep the faith you have to yourself before God. Blessed is the one who does not condemn himself in what he approves. But whoever doubts is condemned if he eats, because he does not act from faith, and whatever does not come from faith is sin." Does anyone need an interpreter to understand both why the apostle said this and how maliciously these men pluck particular bits out of Scripture to trap the unlearned? The apostle said that all things are clean according to faith. He also said that they are unclean to anyone who thinks them unclean, and that we should abstain from them when they are taken in a way that causes offense. That happens when some weak person thinks he must abstain from all meat so as not to come upon meat sacrificed to idols. He may then suppose that someone who eats does so in honor of idols, and be gravely offended by it, even though sacrificial meat itself defiles no one if someone who does not know what it is receives it in faith. That is why, in another place, the same apostle forbids asking questions when something is bought from the market, or when someone invited to an unbeliever's house sees meat served at his table. These men consider such meat unclean, not because it has been sacrificed but simply because it is meat. Yet the apostle proclaims that all things are clean, that every creature of God is good, and that all things are sanctified by the word and by prayer. He also says that we should abstain from them if some weak person happens to be offended. And in one place he pointed to these men quite plainly, when he says that in the last times there will be some who forbid marriage and abstain from foods that God created. Here he is describing precisely those who abstain from such foods, not to curb their own desires or to spare someone else's weakness, but because they think meat itself is unclean and deny that God is its creator. Let us, however, hold to the apostle's teaching, which says that all things are clean to the clean, while keeping the moderation of the Gospel, so that our hearts are not weighed down with overindulgence and drunkenness and the cares of this world.

The same apostle also says, "You cannot share in the table of the Lord and the table of demons." I do not see why the Manichees thought they should set this against this passage of the Law as if it contradicted it. When Deuteronomy says, "According to the desire of your soul, kill and eat all meat, according to the pleasure that the Lord has given you," the Law is not speaking about sacrifices. It is speaking about foods that serve to nourish human beings. But the Manichees say that even when animals are prepared for someone's dinner, that is a sacrifice, and by their way of understanding they took these passages to be contradictory. That is why they also cited the place where the apostle says, "What the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God." Yet the apostle was speaking quite plainly about victims offered to demons in temples, not about the food people prepare for themselves. This is what he says: "What then? Do I say that what is sacrificed to idols is anything, or that an idol is anything? No, but what they sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God. I do not want you to become partners with demons. You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot share in the table of the Lord and the table of demons. Or are we provoking the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than he is? All things are lawful, but not all things are beneficial. All things are lawful, but not all things build up. Let no one seek his own good, but the good of the other. Eat whatever is sold in the market without asking questions for the sake of conscience, for the earth is the Lord's, and everything in it. If one of the unbelievers invites you and you wish to go, eat whatever is set before you without raising questions for the sake of conscience. But if someone says to you, 'This has been sacrificed,' do not eat it, for the sake of the one who told you and for the sake of conscience. I mean not your own conscience but the other person's. For why should my freedom be judged by someone else's conscience? If I partake with thanksgiving, why am I denounced over something for which I give thanks? So whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God." Let the Manichees pay attention to this and see in what sense Deuteronomy said, "According to the desire of your soul, kill and eat all meat, according to the pleasure that the Lord has given you." The Jews were commanded not to eat certain meats, and these were called unclean. This serves to signify unclean people, who were marked out by figures in the old Scriptures. The ox that the Law forbids to be muzzled while it threshes signifies the evangelist, as the apostle explains quite plainly. In the same way, the forbidden foods signify certain impurities in human beings that are not received into the fellowship of Christ's body, that is, into the stable and everlasting Church. For as far as food is concerned, it is perfectly clear that nothing at all is unclean, but that it is wrong for a person to eat in a way that causes offense.

On what is written in Leviticus: "Separate the unclean from the clean, and let no one eat the flesh of the camel, the donkey, the hare, the pig, the eagle, the kite, the raven, the vulture, and the rest." This man has thrown up passages from the two Testaments as though they were opposed and contrary to each other, and his soul is full of tricks and deceit. Nowhere can it be caught more plainly than here, where he mentions that Leviticus commands abstinence from the flesh of certain animals. He thought this saying should be countered by the passage in the Gospel where the Lord says: "Nothing that enters a person defiles him, but the things that come out of him defile him." If he did this without realizing it, nothing could be blinder; if he did it knowingly, nothing could be more wicked. Had he not himself, a little earlier, cited the testimony of the apostle saying, "It is good, brothers, not to eat meat or drink wine," when he wanted to set the New Testament against the Old, where it is said, "According to the desire of your soul, kill and eat all meat"? Why, then, is he now pleased with the Lord's saying that nothing entering a person defiles him, but that what comes out of a person defiles him? Where will he hide from this saying? Where will he run? Let him tell me, when, out of a perverse and superstitious notion of continence, he commands that unclean meats be shunned and kept apart from the food of the saints. Certainly, if it is true that what enters a person does not defile him, then the Manichees are badly mistaken when they call it unclean food when people eat meat. But if such foods are unclean, what will they do with this testimony, which comes with the divine authority of the Gospel, where the Lord says that a person is not defiled by what enters him but by what comes out of him? Will they perhaps say, as they usually do when the authority of Scripture presses them, that corrupters of the Scriptures inserted this chapter into the Gospel? Then why does Adimantus call this chapter as a witness and try to use it to attack the Old Testament, when it is what knocks him down? For a Catholic Christian who reveres and understands both Scriptures will answer him that these passages are not contrary. The precepts about the flesh of certain animals, which a people that was still carnal was commanded not to eat, were set down to signify human ways of life. The Church, which is the Lord's body, cannot receive these into the stable and everlasting bond of its unity. It spits them out like unclean food and does not take them into its own body. In this way all those precepts laid upon a carnal people foretold the future discipline of a spiritual people. They therefore do not conflict with the Lord's saying, in which he says with perfect truth that a person is not defiled by what enters him as food. The one saying lays burdens on slaves; the other now shakes the yoke of slavery off those who are free. Yet the first was spoken in such a way that the burdens of the slaves foretold the faith of the free. For, as the apostle says, all these things happened to them as figures, for our sake, upon whom the end of the ages has come. If, then, what they suffered happened as a figure, the instructions they were given were also received as a figure.

Once I have given this answer, and shown in this way that these two passages taken from the two Testaments are not contrary, what will this man do, when the witness he himself brought forward against his adversary gives the weightiest testimony against him? For he himself cited the testimony of the Gospel, where the Lord says that a man is not defiled by the foods that go into him; and yet he never stops urging and teaching that people must abstain from meat as from unclean food. Still, he sensed how great a wound he was inflicting on himself, and how hard the blow was that would rebound and injure him. Someone might question him and say: "How, then, do you forbid eating meat, if the Lord says, as you yourself cite, 'Nothing that goes into a man defiles him, but the things that come out of him defile him'?" So he wanted to apply a kind of remedy to a mortal wound, but to no purpose. This is how he set out that Gospel testimony: "In the Gospel," he says, "the Lord says to the crowd: Hear and understand: nothing that goes into a man defiles him," and so on. His mention that the Lord said this to the crowd shows only that he did what he did not out of ignorance but out of malice, so that he could later tell his hearers that the Lord spoke these words to the crowd, not to the few holy ones such as the Manichees themselves wish to appear. They allow their hearers, as people still unclean, to eat meat, while they consider it criminal and wicked for themselves, as people already clean. So he wanted it to look as though the Lord meant the same thing, since he taught this not to a few holy ones but to crowds. O most wicked man, so confident that the human race would be careless enough to let him hide his deceptions! He did not believe anyone would take up the Gospel, read what follows, and find a man hiding snares for the unwary and the less careful in the very pastures where the Lord feeds his flocks. For the disciples were troubled by these words, and believed that the Lord had spoken figuratively rather than literally when he said that a man is not defiled by what goes into him as food. The disciples too were Jews, after all, and had received from childhood an ingrained habit of avoiding certain kinds of meat. So they came to him and said: "Do you know that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this saying?" He answered: "Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted. Let them alone: they are blind, and leaders of the blind. And if the blind lead the blind, both fall into the pit." He thus called the unbelief of the Jews a plant that the heavenly Father had not planted. Peter, however, still thought it was a parable, and that the Jews had been rebuked and called blind because they could not understand it. So he answered and said to him: "Explain this parable to us." And the Lord, showing as plainly as possible that it was not a parable but a literal statement, said to them: "Are you also still without understanding? Do you not understand that whatever enters the mouth goes into the belly and is cast out into the drain? But what comes out of the mouth comes from the heart, and that is what defiles a man. For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witness, blasphemies; these are what defile a man. But to eat with unwashed hands does not defile a man." The Jews had raised a question about unwashed hands, and on that occasion the Lord pronounced a general judgment about the things that enter the mouth, go into the belly, and are cast out into the drain, that is, about our food. It is true that Scripture says he called the crowds to him and said, "Not what enters the mouth defiles a man, but what comes out of the mouth." Yet it is clear enough why this man, out of fear, added that detail to the words with which he cited this testimony. As was said a little earlier, he wanted an answer for those who might ask him why the leaders of the Manichees think it a sin for themselves to eat meat: namely, that the Lord's saying would seem to be a concession to the crowds only, not to the elect. But what follows makes it plain that the Lord gave the same answer to Peter when he asked privately, with the disciples listening, the very men he was raising to the summit of the Church. In this way he testified that he had not said these things in a parable, and he showed that they apply to everyone. So these people have no grounds for snatching food out of men's mouths and binding them in the snare of superstition.

Perhaps one of them will say: "Then explain what is signified by the flesh of the pig, the camel, the hare, the kite, the raven, and the rest, from which the Law commands abstinence." I will not, because it would take too long. But suppose I could not: does it follow that no one can? There are already countless volumes in which these things have been explained. For refuting these people, however, it is enough for us that it is not I but the Apostle who says that these observances are a shadow of things to come. He forbids observing them in a slavish way, yet he declares that they signify something, when he says: "Let no one, then, judge you in food or in drink, or with regard to a feast day or a new moon or sabbaths, which are a shadow of things to come." So once those future realities signified by these observances had come through Christ, the Lord of the laws, the slavish observances were removed, but their interpretations are kept by the free. For whatever signified the Church that was to come is prophecy. And you have the same Apostle saying: "Do not quench the Spirit; do not despise prophecy; read all things; hold fast to what is good." So divine Scripture must be read, the dispensation of the Holy Spirit must be recognized, and prophecy must be looked into; carnal slavery must be rejected and the understanding proper to the free retained.

On what is written in Deuteronomy: "Observe and sanctify the day, as the Lord commanded you. Six days you shall labor and do all your work, but on the seventh day, the sabbath, you shall feast to the Lord your God, doing no work, neither you nor your son nor your daughter nor your manservant nor your maidservant, your ox and your donkey and all your beasts, and your tenant. Let your manservant and your maidservant rest just as you do. Remember that you were a slave in Egypt, and the Lord your God brought you out with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm. That is why the Lord commanded you to keep the seventh day." And again it is written in Genesis, where God speaks to Abraham about circumcision: "Keep my covenant," he says, "you and your descendants after you. This is my covenant, which you shall keep between me and you and your descendants: you shall circumcise every male in the flesh of their foreskin, and this shall be the sign of the covenant between me and you. On the eighth day you shall circumcise every male in your nation, including the one born in your house and the one bought with money, except the foreigner; and this shall be the covenant in your nation. And every male who does not circumcise his foreskin shall lose his soul from the midst of the people, because he has broken my covenant." Adimantus sets out all these words of the Old Testament in order to set the New Testament against them, and he claims that they are contrary to what the Lord says in the Gospel about the proselyte: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, for you travel around sea and land to make a single proselyte, and when you have made him, he becomes a son of hell far more than you are."
