As if the Lord called the proselyte a son of hell because he is circumcised and keeps the sabbath, and not rather because he is forced to imitate the depraved morals and perverse way of life of the Jews: not where they keep the precepts of the Law, but where they act against the Law. He says this about them very plainly in another place, where he says that they reject the commandment of God in order to establish their own tradition: although the Law commanded that father and mother be honored, they themselves laid down ways in which parents might be dishonored. Again, he says to them: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who have the keys of the kingdom of heaven; you neither enter yourselves nor allow others to enter." And in another place he commanded his hearers to obey the words of the scribes and Pharisees but not to imitate their deeds. For he says: "They sit on the chair of Moses; do what they say, but do not do what they do, for they say and do not do." In this passage the Lord both confirms the authority of the Law given through Moses and shows very plainly that the morals of those who did not obey the Law they had received must be guarded against and shunned. Through these perversities of theirs they brought it about that when some Gentile had gone over to their Law, that is, had become a proselyte, he took on their morals and became a son of hell far more than they were. For they took great pains to make someone from among the Gentiles a Jew, and once he had become a Jew they compelled him to imitate their own very wicked ways.

Nor could Adimantus see that the passage he cites from the Apostle as contrary is not contrary at all, because his whole eye was fixed not on inquiring into Scripture but on finding fault with it. He cites the Apostle saying: "Was anyone called when circumcised? Let him not restore his foreskin. Was anyone called in uncircumcision? Let him not be circumcised; for uncircumcision is nothing and circumcision is nothing, but keeping the commandments of God." What could be clearer than that the Apostle is commanding here that each person remain as he was when called? For when the realities came of which those observances were shadows, the point was to show that hope must be placed not in the shadows themselves but in the realities those shadows signified as coming, that is, Christ and the Church. That is why all those things were now empty. Yet the Apostle commands not that they be removed as harmful, but that they be disregarded as superfluous. So if a Jew had believed in Christ, he was not forbidden to remain in those superfluous practices, to avoid giving offense to his own people, though he was not to think that his salvation rested on them. For it is not those signs that bring us to salvation, but the things signified by them. Therefore uncircumcision is nothing and circumcision is nothing, but keeping the commandments of God. And when he says in another place, "I wish that those who are unsettling you would even cut themselves off," the Apostle does not say this because circumcision is contrary to the Gospel, as the Manichees think. What is contrary to the Gospel is for someone to abandon the reality prefigured by that shadow and follow the emptiness of the shadow itself. This is what was wanted by those who imposed the yoke of circumcision on Gentiles believing in Christ as if it were necessary for salvation, at a time when there was no longer a shadow to be figured in the body, but the reality itself to be carried in the heart.

And as for his saying, "You observe days and sabbaths and festivals; I fear for you, that I may have labored over you in vain," this is not actually written as Adimantus quotes it. The Apostle does not mention the sabbath there. What he says is: "You observe days and years and seasons; I fear for you, that I may have labored over you in vain." But suppose it were said about the sabbath. Do we not say as well that these things are not to be observed, but rather the things they signify? For those people observed them slavishly, without understanding what realities they signified and foretold. This is what the Apostle blames in them, and in all who serve the creature rather than the Creator. We too solemnly observe the Lord's Day and Easter and any other Christian festivals; but because we understand what they point to, we do not observe the seasons themselves but what those seasons signify. The Manichees, however, criticize these things as if they themselves observed no days or seasons. Yet when they are questioned about them, they try to explain everything according to the teaching of their sect, so that they appear to observe not the seasons themselves but the realities of which they are signs. That those realities are fables and utter falsehoods is shown elsewhere. Here it is said only so that they may be forced to admit with their own mouths that such things can be celebrated rationally. It is therefore clear that circumcision of the flesh was rightly imposed on slaves and rightly understood by the free. So with the Apostle we reject it in its carnal form, and with the Apostle we approve it in its spiritual form. We do not observe the sabbath rest in time, but we understand it as a temporal sign, and we direct the eye of the heart toward the eternal rest that this sign signifies. So with the Apostle we reject the observance of seasons, and with the Apostle we keep the understanding of temporal signs. And we accept the difference between the two Testaments in this way: in the one are the burdens of slaves, in the other the joys of the free; in the one our possession is recognized in prefiguration, in the other the possession itself is held. The Apostle interprets the sabbath in the Letter to the Hebrews when he says: "There remains, therefore, a sabbath rest for the people of God." He also interprets circumcision when he says of Abraham: "And he received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness of faith." So I hold to the Apostle's interpretation spiritually, and in freedom I disregard the carnal observance of slavery, revering God as the author of both Testaments. As a master, he set before the old man in his flight something to fear; and as a father, he opened to the new man on his return something to love.

On what is written in Exodus: "If you listen with your ear to my voice and do whatever I command you, I will hate those who hate you and afflict those who afflict you. My angel will go before you and bring you to the Amorites and the Perizzites and the Canaanites and the Jebusites and the Girgashites, and you shall kill them. You shall not worship their gods or do their works, but you shall utterly overthrow them and blot out their memory." After citing these words from the old books, Adimantus sets against them, as contrary, what is written in the Gospel, where the Lord says: "But I say to you, love your enemies, bless those who curse you, and do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute you." The first thing to notice here is that, for a man who wanted to show contradictions, it should have been enough to point out what is written in the old law about killing enemies. For the Lord's command to love our enemies certainly concerned human beings, and anyone can see, and it has very often been shown by examples, that they can be converted to salvation through our patience and love. Why, then, did he think he should add what follows, where it is written, "You shall not worship their gods or do their works, but utterly overthrow them and blot out their memory," unless the Manichees also compel us to love the gods of the Gentiles? Do they think that what the Lord says in the Gospel, "Love your enemies," applies not only to human beings but also to demons, or even to idols? If so, who would not detest such madness? But if they do not think so, then this man went badly astray when he chose to cite the Old Testament command that the superstitions of the Gentiles be overthrown, in order to set against it, as contrary, what is written in the New about loving our enemies.

We, however, do not say that what was told to that people in the old books about killing enemy men is contrary to this gospel precept, by which the Lord commands us to love our enemies. That killing of enemies still suited a carnal people, to whom the law had been given as a kind of guardian, as the apostle says. As for those who were then holy and spiritual men in that people (they were very few, like Moses, like the prophets), the intention with which they carried out that killing of enemies, and whether they loved those whom they killed, is wholly hidden from the unlearned and the ungodly, who love their own blindness. Since they are not fit to see these things, they must rather be pressed by the weight of authority. For what does the apostle mean when he says: "For my part, though absent in body but present in spirit, I have already judged, as though present, the man who has done this: in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when you and my spirit are gathered together with the power of our Lord Jesus, to hand such a one over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus"? For what does that killing, which these people so greatly exaggerate and spread about to stir up ill will, amount to except the destruction of the flesh? But since the apostle explained with what intention he acted, he made it plain enough that vengeance can proceed against an enemy together with love. And yet here, perhaps, the destruction of the flesh can also be understood in another way, as the destruction that comes about through repentance. They themselves, moreover, read apocryphal scriptures, which they even claim are wholly uncorrupted, where it is written that the apostle Thomas cursed a man who had rashly struck him with the palm of his hand, not knowing who he was, and that the curse took effect at once. For when that man, who was a servant at the banquet, had gone out to the spring to fetch water, he was killed and torn to pieces by a lion. And so that this might be made known to terrify others, a dog carried his hand to the tables where the apostle was dining. And so, when those who did not know asked the cause and it was explained to them, they were turned to great fear of the apostle and great honour for him, and from this arose the first beginning of the gospel's being commended. If anyone wanted to turn the Manichees' teeth against themselves, how bitingly he would censure these things! But because there too it is not left unsaid with what intention it was done, the love of the one taking vengeance can be seen. For this is what one reads in that scripture: that the apostle prayed for the man on whom temporal vengeance had been taken, that he might be spared at the judgement to come. If, then, in the time of the New Testament, when love is especially commended, God struck fear into carnal people through visible punishments, how much more must we understand that this suited that people in the time of the Old Testament, whom fear of the law restrained like a guardian? For this is the briefest and plainest difference between the two testaments: fear and love. The one belongs to the old man, the other to the new, yet both were brought forth and joined together by the most merciful dispensation of the one God. And in the old scripture the intention of those who took vengeance is passed over in silence, because the very few spiritual men knew through divine revelations what they were doing, so that the people, for whom terror was useful, might be tamed by the strictest command. Just as they saw ungodly enemies and worshippers of idols given into their hands to be killed, so they themselves would dread being given into the hands of their enemies if they despised the commands of the true God and slipped into the worship of idols and the impieties of the gentiles. For when they themselves sinned in the same way, vengeance was taken on them in the same way. But all this temporal vengeance terrifies weak minds, so that it may instruct those brought up under discipline and turn them away from eternal and unspeakable punishments; for carnal people fear what God punishes in the present more than what he threatens for the future.

There can, then, be love in one who punishes. Everyone proves this in his own son, when the boy is sliding into the worst habits and he restrains him with the strictest discipline, all the more strictly the more he loves him, judging that he can be corrected in this way. People do not, however, kill the sons they love when they wish to correct them, because many regard this life as a great good, and the whole reason they wish to bring up their sons lies in their hopes for this life. Faithful and wise people, too, who believe there is another and better life and know it in part as far as they can, do not punish by killing when they wish to correct their sons, because they believe that their sons can be corrected in this life. But God, who knows what to allot to each, punishes by killing whomever he wills, whether through human beings or through the hidden order of things. He does this not because he hates them insofar as they are human beings, but insofar as they are sinners. For in those very old books we read it said to God: "And you hate none of the things you have made." Rather, he disposes all things, whether by punishments or by rewards, with justice governing. Was not the apostle Paul speaking to faithful Christians when he said: "Let a man examine himself, and so eat of the bread and drink of the cup. For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgement on himself, not discerning the Lord's body. That is why many among you are weak and sick, and a good number have fallen asleep. But if we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged. But when we are judged, we are chastened by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned along with this world"? See, it is plain that God lovingly corrects those whom he does not wish to condemn with the world, not only with weakness and sickness but even with temporal death.

Let these people pay attention to this. Let them see how even ungodly nations could be given into the hands of a people that, though still carnal, nevertheless worshipped the one God, to be killed by it, while in that people any who were spiritual understood God's dispensation without hatred toward anyone. And let them see how this is not contrary to what the Lord commanded us in the gospel, that we should love our enemies. For he himself nevertheless promises vengeance on them, when he tells the parable of the judge who was unjust, neither fearing God nor respecting people, yet could not bear the daily pleas of a widow asking him to avenge her, and heard her so as not to be troubled any further. By comparison with him, the Lord said, God, who is most kind and most just, will all the more avenge his children on their enemies. Let them dare to put this question to him and say, if they can: "Why did you command us to love our enemies, when you arrange to avenge us on them?" Or will he perhaps act against the will of his saints by punishing and condemning those whom they love? Rather, let them turn from this slanderous blindness to God and understand his will in both testaments, so that they may not be found on the left side among those to whom the Lord will say: "Depart into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry and you gave me nothing to eat," and the rest of that passage. For these wretched people are displeased that God handed enemies over to his people to be killed, and yet they themselves forbid bread to be given to a beggar, who is not an enemy but a suppliant. Let them rather understand that there can be vengeance without hatred, something few understand. And yet, as long as it is not understood, the reader of the books of both testaments must be tossed about by great toil or error and think that the scriptures contradict one another.

The apostles had not yet grasped in their minds this vengeance without hatred when, angry with those who would not receive them as guests, they asked the Lord whether he wanted them to call down fire from heaven, as Elijah had done, so that those inhospitable people would be consumed by it. Then the Lord answered them, saying that they did not know whose spirit they were children of, and that he had come to save, not to destroy; for they, with hostile minds, desired to destroy those whom they wanted consumed by fire. Later, however, when they had been filled with the Holy Spirit and made perfect, so that they could now even love their enemies, they received the power to punish, because they could now punish without hatred. The apostle Peter used this power in that book which these people do not accept, because it plainly contains the coming of the Paraclete, that is, of the Comforter, the Holy Spirit. The Lord sent him to those who were mourning, after he himself had ascended into heaven out of their sight. For a comforter is sent to the sorrowful, in keeping with that saying of the same Lord: "Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted." He also said: "Then the sons of the bridegroom will mourn, when the bridegroom is taken away from them." In that book, then, where the coming of the Holy Spirit, whom the Lord had promised as Comforter, is most plainly declared, we read that at Peter's sentence people fell down and died: a husband and wife who had dared to lie to the Holy Spirit. In their great blindness these people find fault with this, while in the apocrypha they read as a great deed both what I mentioned about the apostle Thomas and the stories that Peter's own daughter was made paralysed by her father's prayers and that a gardener's daughter died at Peter's own prayer. They reply that this was for their good, that the one should be struck with paralysis and the other should die; yet they do not deny that it was done at the apostle's prayers. But who told them that it was not for the good of the ungodly nations to be killed? Mockingly, they pretend to be amazed that those nations were handed over by God into the hands of the Jewish people. Since the apostles did those things not out of hatred but with good intent, on what grounds do these people convict the spiritual men who lived in that people of hating those whom divine justice commanded to be removed from this life through them? Let them rather restrain their own rashness and not deceive the inexperienced: those who either have no time to read, or do not want to read, or read with a perverse mind and fail to notice that both the mercy and the severity of God are commended in the writings of both testaments. For on love of one's enemy, so that evil is not repaid with evil, do we not read in the old books: "O Lord my God, if I have done this, if there is iniquity in my hands, if I have repaid with evil those who repaid me, may I deservedly fall empty before my enemies"? Who would say this except someone who knew that it pleases God that no one should repay evil with evil? But it belongs to the perfect to hate nothing in sinners except their sins while loving the people themselves, and, when they punish, to punish not with harsh cruelty but with the moderation of justice, so that the very letting-off of the sin may not harm the sinner more than the punishment of vengeance. Yet righteous men did not do this except by divine authority, so that no one may think he is permitted at will to kill whomever he likes, or to prosecute him in court, or to afflict him with any punishment whatever. Sometimes this divine authority is openly set down in the scriptures, and sometimes it is hidden, so that the reader may be instructed by what is plain and exercised by what is obscure.

Certainly David had King Saul, his enemy and persecutor, exceedingly ungrateful and exceedingly hostile, delivered into his power, to do with him as he wished; and he chose to spare him rather than kill him. He had not been commanded to kill, but neither had he been forbidden. Indeed, he had even heard from God that he could do whatever he wished to his enemy with impunity, and yet he turned so great a power to gentleness. Let someone tell me whom he feared when he refused to kill. We cannot say that he feared the man, who had been delivered into his power, or God, who had delivered him. Where, then, there was neither difficulty in killing nor fear, love spared the enemy. See: David the warrior fulfilled the precept of Christ which we have received, that we should love our enemies. If only these people would imitate this, they who have twisted the human feeling of compassion into who knows what cruel ravings! For while they believe that bread weeps, which cannot happen, they will not hand it to a human being whom they see weeping. Perhaps they will say, in the way the blind usually hurl insane insults, that David, who spared his enemy, was better than God, who had given him the power to kill, as if God did not know to whom he was giving this power. He certainly knew his servant's will. But so that the love of his enemy that God already knew to be in David's heart might also become known to other people for them to imitate, he gave into David's power the enemy whom he did not yet wish to be killed, because of a fixed ordering of events that had to be fulfilled through Saul. Thus David's goodness was commended, so that people would have something to love, and Saul's wickedness was kept for a more fitting end, so that people would have something to fear.

On what is written in Deuteronomy: "If you listen with your ear to the voice of the Lord your God, you are blessed in your field, you are blessed in your meadow; blessed is the fruit of your womb and the fruit of your land, and the offspring of your beasts, and the herd of your cattle, and the flock of your sheep; you are blessed in your coming in and your going out." They say that this passage in the gospel is contrary to it: "If anyone wishes to follow me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me. For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul? Or what will a man give in exchange for his soul?" But it is shown not to be contrary by the rule by which it should already be known that carnal and temporal rewards were fittingly promised to a people that was still carnal, yet promised by the one God, to whom all creation, both higher and lower, belongs. Adimantus himself certainly cited a text from the gospel where the Lord says: "Do not swear, either by heaven, for it is his throne, or by the earth, for it is the footstool of his feet." This is indeed written in the old books too: "Heaven is my throne, the earth the footstool of my feet." What wonder is it, then, if he gives the goods of his throne to those who serve him spiritually and the goods of his footstool to those who serve him carnally, since spirit is higher and flesh lower, just as heavenly things are higher and earthly things lower? All those things, the field and the meadow, the fruit of the womb, the fruit of the land and of the beasts, the herd of cattle and the flock of sheep, can of course also be understood spiritually, but that discussion is not relevant to the matter now. The New Testament's reward and inheritance belong to the new man. Yet even there the Lord promises those very people whom he wants to despise temporal things, so that they may serve him in the gospel, that those same things will be multiplied in this age, saying that they will receive a hundredfold in this age and eternal life in the age to come. So too it is said in the old scripture: "To the faithful man the whole world is wealth"; and so the apostle exults, saying: "as having nothing, and yet possessing all things." If, then, in the New Testament, besides the eternal possession promised to the saints, the multiplication of this possession that will pass away is not withheld either, and becomes all the more abundant the more lightly it is held, how much more ought such things to have been the rewards of a carnal people in the Old Testament, with the same one true God, the governor of all times, regulating and administering all things as each time required?

But so that they may not think these things are despised only in the books of the New Testament, let them hear the prophet rejecting such happiness and singing that we must take refuge in the one Lord God. For he says: "Rescue me from the wicked sword and deliver me from the hand of foreign sons, whose mouth has spoken emptiness, and whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity. Their sons are like young plants firmly set in their youth; their daughters are adorned and decked out like the likeness of a temple; their storehouses are full, overflowing from one kind of store to another; their sheep are fruitful, multiplying as they go out; their oxen are fat. There is no breach in their wall, no going out, no outcry in their streets. They have called the people happy that has these things; happy is the people whose God is the Lord." Let them notice, then, how this happiness is mocked in ungodly people, and how all blessedness is fixed, unshaken, in God alone. For those people call the people happy that has these things; but happy is the people whose God is the Lord. They have also thought that this saying of the Lord is contrary to this passage of the Old Testament: "Whoever is ashamed of me or of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, the Son of Man will also be ashamed of him when he comes in the glory of his Father and the praise of his holy angels." I do not see what this has to do with contempt for temporal things. But if it is relevant in this sense, that no one should be frightened by the loss of such things into being ashamed or afraid to confess Christ, what do they have to say? For we too say that these things are gifts of God, though the lowest of gifts, and that compared with the confession that brings salvation they must be not only lost but even willingly thrown away. Yet the Lord God usefully promised them to carnal people, who loved them and could not yet grasp the heavenly promises, so that they would not seek them from idols and demons.

On what is written in the law: "I am he who gives riches to my friends and poverty to my enemies." Against this saying they set what the Lord says: "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven," and: "Woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation." But why will they not look at other things in the gospel too? For where it is written, "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven," there follows: "Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth as their inheritance." See, there they have God's friends being made rich with the inheritance of the earth. And when that rich man is reduced to such want that he begs for moisture to be dripped onto his parched tongue from the tip of a finger dipped in water by the poor man he had neglected, let them understand how God's enemies become poor, and recognize that this is what is written in the law: "I am he who gives riches to my friends and poverty to my enemies."

For I have shown above that these temporal riches are despised in the old scripture as well, and anyone who wishes to read it will find this in countless places. From there come these words too: "Better is a little for the righteous man than the many riches of sinners"; and: "The law of your mouth is better to me than thousands of gold and silver"; and: "The judgements of God are true, justified in themselves, more desirable than gold and much precious stone"; and: "Blessed is the man who finds wisdom, and immortal is he who sees understanding. For it is better to trade for her than for treasures of gold and silver; she is more precious than the finest stones; no evil withstands her; she is well known to all who draw near to her and to those who consider her carefully. Nothing precious is worthy of her"; and: "Therefore I prayed, and understanding was given to me; I called upon God, and the spirit of wisdom came upon me. I preferred her to sceptres and thrones, and counted honour as nothing in comparison with her. Nor did I compare any precious stone to her, for all gold in comparison with her is a little sand, and silver will be reckoned as mud beside her." If these people read these things, or did not read them with an ungodly mind, they would see that everything in the scriptures of both testaments, both what is to be sought and what is to be shunned, what is to be taken up and what is to be rejected, agrees together and is arranged in its proper order of rank.

On what is written in the law: "If you walk in the law and keep my commandments, I will give you rain in its season, and the land will bring forth its fruits and the trees their apples, and your vintage will follow your harvest, and your sowing your vintage; and you will be filled, and you will dwell in peace in your land, and you will sleep, and there will be no one to make you afraid. I will destroy every wild beast from your land, and you will pursue your enemies, and they will fall before you by the sword. Five of you will chase a hundred, and a hundred of you will pursue ten thousand, and your enemies will fall before you by the sword. And I will come and bless you and multiply you and establish you. You will eat the old store, long kept, and you will throw out the old to make room for the new." By now no one ought to ask us to show how fittingly God promised these things to that people. We have said a great deal about this, and anyone who thinks it too little is far too slow. Still, they also say that something in the New Testament is contrary to this passage, namely what the Lord says: "Do not carry gold or silver or coins in your belts, no bag for the journey, nor two tunics, nor sandals, nor a staff; for the labourer is worthy of his wages." What wonder is it if he granted these things to the evangelists? Was the Jewish people called to this ministry? Yet all these things must be examined spiritually, so that the ungodly may not think that the Lord himself acted against his own commands, for he also kept a purse in which money was carried for necessary food. Unless perhaps they are going to say that keeping money in belts is a sin, but keeping it in a purse is not. That these things were not commanded but permitted to the apostles can be understood from the fact that the apostle Paul earned his living by working with his own hands, not making use of the right, as he himself says, which the Lord gave to the evangelists. For what the Lord permits, one may also leave undone; but what he commands is a sin if it is not done.

They also bring up the rich man to whom God had said: "Fool, this night I will demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?" They say that this too is contrary to this chapter of the law. But in that case what was mocked was the emptiness of a vain rejoicing, because the man treated uncertain things as certain. For the people of Israel, on the other hand, the omnipotence of the one who promised made that promise certain. That is why the apostle Paul, writing to Timothy about the rich of this world, whom he knew to have their own place among the members of the church, speaks as follows: "Command the rich of this world not to be proud, and not to set their hope on the uncertainty of riches but on the living God, who provides us richly with all things to enjoy. Let them do good, be rich in good works, give readily and share, and store up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may lay hold of true life." Who would not understand from this that it is not blameworthy to have these things? What is blameworthy is to love them and put one's hope in them, and to prefer them to, or even compare them with, truth, justice, wisdom, faith, a good conscience, and the love of God and neighbor. In these every devout soul is rich in its hidden depths before the eyes of God. God bestows all these invisible and eternal things on those who love him. That is, he gives himself, full of all of them, to those who love him. In order, then, that he may be loved even at the time when the carnal soul, entangled in the affections of the flesh, knows how to desire nothing but earthly and temporal things, that soul must be persuaded that God gives even these things to human beings. This is both true and most useful to believe. This was done for the people of Israel through those promises which these wretched men so ignorantly deride, so that even in these lowest things they might, in whatever way they could, grow used to loving God, although fear was more at work there. Yet all these temporal gifts are figures of eternal gifts, and that victory over enemies foreshadows the victory over the devil and his angels.

They have also added, as though it were contrary to the Old Testament, that the apostle says God delights not in strife and dissension but in peace. Let them know that the God proclaimed in those scriptures is one whose peace no one can take away. He is not like the god they proclaim, who was afraid that war would burst upon his realms and sent his own members far away to endure foreign wars. Afterward he could not free and cleanse them once they had been conquered and defiled. In human nature, which slid down through sin to lower things, God delights in peace in this way: he does not abandon the balance of justice. Nor does he want the peace he loves to be trampled by sinners. He wants it to be loved by those who strive and grasped by those who conquer. He promises it in figures to the carnal and shows it openly to the spiritual.

On what is written in Deuteronomy: "Cursed is everyone who has hung on a tree." The Manichees have often aired this question. Even so, I do not see what in the gospel passage that Adimantus thought he should set against this statement is contrary to it. There the Lord says: "If you wish to be perfect, sell all that you possess and divide it among the poor, and take up your cross and follow me." Apart from the fact that the Lord names the cross here, Adimantus finds nothing contrary to the saying "Cursed is everyone who has hung on a tree." As if anyone could take up a cross of that kind and follow the Lord! The cross we take up when we follow the Lord is the one of which the apostle says: "Those who belong to Jesus Christ have crucified their flesh with its passions and desires." By such a cross the old man is put to death, that is, the old life that we drew from Adam. What was voluntary in him became natural in us, as the apostle shows when he says: "We too were once by nature children of wrath, like the rest." So the old life comes from Adam, and that is why it is signified by the name "the old man." What, then, is absurd about the curse being pronounced on the old man, whom the Lord hung on the tree? Through that same line of descent the Lord bore mortality, for he was born mortal of the Virgin Mary. His flesh was not sinful, but it still bore the likeness of sinful flesh, because it could die, and death comes from sin. Hence also the words: "knowing that our old man was crucified together with him, so that the body of sin might be done away with." So it was not the Lord who deserved the curse through the tongue of Moses, the servant of God. It was death itself, which our Lord did away with by taking it upon himself. It was that death, then, that hung on the tree, the death which came to man through the woman at the persuasion of the serpent. That is also why Moses lifted up a serpent on a pole in the desert to signify that very death. We are healed of our deadly desires through faith in the Lord's cross, by which death was hung on the tree. For that reason those who had been poisoned by the bites of serpents were healed at once when they looked at the serpent that had been fixed and lifted up on the pole. The Lord himself bore witness to this sacred sign when he said: "For just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so must the Son of Man be lifted up." By taking on the kind of death that people regard as most disgraceful, the death of the cross, our Lord Jesus Christ commended his love to us. So the apostle rightly said, to kindle our love for him: "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us; for it is written: Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree." This was so that Christian freedom would fear no death, and not even any kind of death, as Jewish servitude did.

On the man whom God ordered to be stoned because he was found gathering wood on the sabbath. In the gospel the Lord healed a man's withered hand on the sabbath day. That was a divine work, not a human one, and he who commanded and it was done did not depart from rest. So this act is not like the gathering of wood. The man was found doing that on the sabbath day and was stoned at God's command. A great deal has already been said about the servile observance of the sabbath and about the punishment of temporal death. In the time of love God's goodness is most clearly displayed, and in the same way his severity is most clearly displayed in the time of fear. Before the Lord's coming it was not yet fitting to lay bare to the people the sacred meanings of the figures in the law. Those people were not invited to understand what was signified. They were compelled to carry out what was commanded, for they did not yet cleave to God through the spirit but served the law through the flesh. I am amazed that these people lament the man stoned at God's command for gathering wood against the law's command. Yet they do not lament the tree withered by Christ's word, which had broken no commandment, even though they believe that a tree has the same kind of soul as a human being.

On what is written: "Let your wife be like a flourishing vine, and your children like young olive shoots around your table, and you shall see your children's children; and you will know that this is how the man who fears the Lord is blessed." The prophet spoke this figuratively, and it refers to the church. The Manichees do not understand this. They think it is contrary to what the Lord says in the gospel about eunuchs who castrate themselves for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. But we have already discussed husband, wife and eunuchs as far as was needed in the third chapter.

On what is written in Solomon: "Imitate the ant and consider its diligence, for from summertime until winter it gathers food for itself." The Manichees do not understand that this too must be taken spiritually. They think it is a command to store up treasure on earth, or even to look after those granaries that people hurry to fill with no command at all. That is why Adimantus says that the gospel passage where the Lord says "Do not be anxious about tomorrow" is opposed to this statement. But they do not understand that this saying is meant to keep us from loving temporal things, or from fearing that we will lack necessities, or from serving God or human beings for the sake of acquiring them. Suppose it had been said so that no bread would be kept for the next day. Then it would be better fulfilled by the vagrants of Rome whom they call "pasgivi" [?]. Once their bellies are filled with the daily ration, they either give away at once whatever is left or throw it out. They would fulfill it better than the Lord's disciples, who kept a money bag even while walking on earth with the Lord of heaven and earth himself. They would also fulfill it better than the apostle Paul. He despised all earthly things, yet he managed what was necessary for this present life so carefully that he even gave instructions about widows: "If any believer has widows, let him provide for them adequately, so that the church is not burdened and can provide for those who are truly widows." The saying about the ant is put this way for a reason. The ant gathers in summer what will feed it in winter. In the same way every Christian should gather the word of God in times of calm, which summer signifies. Then in adversity and tribulation, which the word "winter" signifies, he will have something to live on spiritually. For man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God. And if it bothers them that the ant hides what it gathers in the ground, let them also be angry at the treasure which the Lord says was found in a field.

On what is written in Hosea: "Give them an empty womb and dry breasts; put to death the seed of their womb, so that they may not bear." This prophetic saying is certainly figurative too. In the gospel these people do not take "belly" to mean a belly of flesh when they read: "Rivers of living water will flow from his belly." The apostle also had breasts of a kind when he said: "I gave you milk to drink, not solid food." He said again: "I became a little child among you, like a nurse cherishing her own children." And when the Galatians turned aside to other things, he was in labor with them again until Christ was formed in them. So what Adimantus quoted from the gospel does not conflict with this prophetic statement: that in the resurrection from the dead they will neither marry nor take wives nor die, but are like the angels of God. This is surely what the eunuchs receive as well, of whom Isaiah speaks: "I will give them a place with a name, far better than sons and daughters; I will give them an everlasting name," he says. So these people should not think that such a reward is promised to the saints only in the gospel. As for the empty womb, the dry breasts and the seed put to death so that they may not bear, they should understand that this was said about the people of whom the apostle says: "Just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so these also oppose the truth, men corrupt in mind and worthless in regard to the faith. But they will not get any further, for their folly will be plain to everyone, as theirs was." When they get no further, then they will have an empty womb, dry breasts and seed put to death. Let these people be so good as to look at themselves in this saying as in a mirror.

On what is written in the prophet Amos: "Can it be that two walking along a road do not recognize each other at all, and that a lion returns to its cub without prey? Will a bird fall to the ground without a fowler? Do they set a snare for no reason, so as to catch nothing? Will a trumpet sound in a city without the people being afraid? So too no evil is done in a city which the Lord will not do." Here "evil" must be understood not as sin but as punishment. The word "evil" is used in two senses: one is the evil a person does, the other is the evil he suffers. What he does is sin, and what he suffers is punishment. So the prophet was speaking about punishments when he said this. Divine providence governs and rules all things, so that when a person does evil because he wants to, he suffers evil that he does not want. These people accuse the prophet for saying this, as though they had never read in the gospel: "Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? Yet not one of them falls to the ground without the will of your Father." God does evil, then, in this sense: what he does is not evil to God himself, but to those he punishes. As far as he himself is concerned, he does good, because everything just is good, and that punishment is just. So there is no contradiction in what Adimantus raises as an objection, that the Lord said: "A good tree produces good fruit, but a bad tree produces bad fruit." Hell is certainly an evil to the one condemned, but God's justice is good, and that punishment is itself fruit from a good tree. The condemned person, through the evils of his sins, has stored up wrath for himself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the just judgment of God, who will repay each one according to his works. These two trees, however, are quite clearly set out as images of two kinds of people, the just and the unjust. Unless a person changes his will, he cannot do good. The Lord teaches elsewhere that this lies within our power, when he says: "Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad." He says this to those who thought they could speak good things although they were evil, that is, produce good fruit although they were bad trees. For he goes on to say: "Hypocrites, how can you speak good things when you are evil?" A bad tree, then, cannot produce good fruit, but it can become a good tree instead of a bad one, so that it bears good fruit. "For you were once darkness," the apostle says, "but now you are light in the Lord." It is as if he said: "You were once bad trees, and so then you could produce nothing but bad fruit. But now you are light in the Lord. Now that you have become good trees, bear good fruit." He continues with this when he says: "Walk as children of light, for the fruit of light is found in all justice and truth, testing what is pleasing to the Lord." In that very chapter of the gospel Adimantus could have noticed in what sense God is said to do evil, if he had not been raging with malicious zeal. For there the Lord says, as Adimantus himself mentioned: "Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire." These are the evils God does, that is, punishments for sinners. He will throw into the fire the trees that persisted in malice and refused to become good, and this is an evil for those trees. But God, as I have often said, does not produce bad fruit, because the punishment of sin is the fruit of justice.

On what is written in the prophet Isaiah: "I am God, who makes peace and creates evils." This too is resolved by the same rule. Adimantus does not find fault with God for saying "I make peace." He finds fault with him for saying "I create evils." Yet the apostle Paul treated these two things together in one passage, and at greater length: "See, then, the goodness and the severity of God: severity toward those who have fallen, but goodness toward you, if you remain in his goodness; otherwise you too will be cut off. And they, if they do not remain in unbelief, will be grafted in, for God is able to graft them in again." In these words of the apostle the goodness of God is plain enough, the goodness by which Isaiah said, "I am God, who makes peace." So is his severity, by which he said, "I create evils." At the same time Paul shows that it lies in our power whether we deserve to be grafted in by his goodness or cut off by his severity. So the gospel is not contrary to Isaiah, as Adimantus thinks, or rather wants others to think, where the Lord says: "Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God." Even from his own side of the comparison he should have recognized that Isaiah too knew the peacemakers are children of God, since God said through him: "I am he who makes peace." But while he fixes his eye on one part in order to misunderstand it, he has blinded himself to the other. Suppose someone else, equally blind, wanted to say that the Old Testament is good, where the Lord says, "I do not desire the death of the sinner so much as that he turn back and live," but that the New Testament is evil, where Christ says, "Go into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels." Would he not fall into the pit and, with doubled malice, drag down with him into the blindness of ignorance everyone who followed him, the untaught and those who do not know the scriptures? But whoever reads with a devout eye finds in the New Testament what these people condemn in the Old, and in the Old what they praise in the New.

On what is written in Isaiah: "And it happened in the year in which King Uzziah died: I saw the Lord sitting on a throne most high, and the house was full of his glory. And around him stood Seraphim, each having six wings: with two they covered his face, and with two his feet." Against this passage Adimantus sets what the apostle says: "To the invisible King of the ages be honor and praise forever." In this question we must ask why he chose to leave out, in Isaiah's vision, the two wings with which the Seraphim flew as they said, "Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts," and why he did not quote the apostle's words in full. For the apostle said: "To the King of the ages, invisible, incorruptible, the only God, be honor and glory for ever and ever." Was he perhaps afraid that the mention of the Trinity would recommend the prophet to the reader, who might then suspect that something great lay hidden there? For it says three times: "Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts." In the apostle, perhaps, he saw that if he had said "to the incorruptible God," he would have been given the reply we now give these people: "What, then, would the race of darkness have done to an incorruptible God if he had refused to fight it?" Or perhaps he had read faulty manuscripts, or the copy in which we read Adimantus himself is faulty. In any case, we should not spend longer on a doubtful matter. We must now ask how the prophet could say that he saw God on a throne most high, and the apostle Paul could truthfully say that God is invisible. So I ask these people whether invisible things can be seen. If they say they can, why do they find fault when the prophet saw the invisible God? If they say they cannot, let them find fault with the apostle himself instead, if they dare. For he says: "Since the creation of the world the invisible things of God have been clearly seen, being understood through the things that have been made." He himself said that they are invisible, and he himself said in turn that they are seen. Are they not forced here to admit that these things are invisible to bodily eyes but visible to the mind? In the same way, then, the prophet saw God, who is invisible to the body, not with the body but in the spirit.

For many kinds of vision are found in the holy Scriptures. One is by the eyes of the body: so Abraham saw three men under the oak of Mamre, Moses saw the fire in the bush, the disciples saw the Lord transfigured on the mountain between Moses and Elijah, and so on. A second is by the spirit, with which we imagine the things we perceive through the body. For when this part of us is taken up by God, many things are revealed to it, not through the eyes of the body or the ears or any other bodily sense, but things like what those senses perceive. So Peter saw that dish let down from heaven with all kinds of animals. Isaiah's vision, which the impious so ignorantly find fault with, is also of this kind. For God is not bounded by a bodily form. Rather, just as many things are said figuratively and not literally, so too many things are shown figuratively. The third kind of vision is by the gaze of the mind, by which truth and wisdom are understood and beheld. Without this kind, the two I described first are either fruitless or even lead into error. When things are shown by God, whether to the bodily senses or to the part of the soul that takes in images of bodily things, and they are not only perceived in these ways but also understood by the mind, then the revelation is complete. To this third kind belongs the vision I mentioned in the apostle's words: "For the invisible things of God, from the creation of the world, are understood and clearly seen through the things that have been made." So that God may be seen with this vision, hearts are cleansed through devout faith and through the [?] practice of the best conduct. What good did it do King Belshazzar to see a hand writing on the wall before his eyes? Because he could not add the mind's sight to that vision, he was still trying to see what he had already seen. But Daniel, gifted with the light of understanding by which such things are grasped, saw with his mind what the king had seen with his body. Again, King Nebuchadnezzar saw a dream with the part of the soul that takes in images of bodies. Because he did not have an eye of the mind fit to see better what he had seen, that is, to understand it, he looked to someone else's sight to interpret his vision, namely that same Daniel's. Yet when Daniel offered to explain it, the king demanded that he first tell him the dream itself, so that he could have sure grounds for believing him. Daniel, by the revelation of the Holy Spirit, saw what the king had seen in his dream with the part that takes in images of bodies, and he beheld with his mind what it meant. Someone who sees visions offered by God, whether with the body alone or also with the part of the spirit that takes in images of bodies, but does not see with the mind, is not a prophet of the true and supreme God. Yet in the Scriptures such things are often found set down as they were seen and not also as they were understood, so that the vision of the mind, which holds all the fruit, might be kept to exercise the readers. But from the many things that are written plainly, it becomes clear to us how the prophets understood the things they set down in their books in the figurative way they were shown to them. For figurative showings belong to the first two kinds of vision, while the simple and literal revelation of things understood and certain belongs to the vision of the mind, that is, of the understanding. Still, the Holy Spirit of the supreme and unchangeable Wisdom presents and governs all these kinds with wonderful and ineffable arrangements. But those people are wretched who slander the prophet for saying that he saw God, and who set against him the apostle's statement that God is invisible. For if someone else were to set against this word of the apostle the word of the Gospel, where the Lord says, "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God," how would they answer that the invisible can be seen? They overwhelm the unlearned with a mere word, and in what sense God is called invisible, even if they know it themselves, they are afraid to have it known. So great is the ruin of minds that, while they want to defeat a man, are themselves defeated by error.
